The writer incorporates a variety of sensory details—particularly sight, sound, and touch—that make the environment feel tangible and real. In the very first paragraph, the reader can feel the boys "rowing" their arms against the resistance of the wind, see the slush ("Eisbrei") splashing around their feet, and hear the rattling ("klapperten") of their school supplies inside sealskin satchels. Later in the passage, the wider town is brought to life through the sounds of the sawmill's machines hissing and spitting ("unter Fauchen und Zischen") by the river, and the visual detail of the grain sacks with "broad black company print" being driven through the streets. These vivid sensory elements successfully immerse the reader in the world of the story.
